title: An Introduction to the Problem-Management Process
overview: Part III opens by arguing that every approach to helping must ultimately help clients manage problems and develop unused opportunities, so Egan adopts a flexible, humanistic problem-management and opportunity-development framework, and reviews the nine ingredients of successful therapy that it organises. Chapter 8 then turns four fundamental client questions into three stages (current picture, preferred picture, way forward), each with three tasks, all resting on an action arrow for implementation. It explains why this is a framework rather than a rigid model, using Kay's idea of obliquity and four points on flexibility (different entry points, different engagement, intermingling stages, flexibility without chaos). It presents Egan's thirteen-step combination of Yankelovich's and Prochaska's stages of change and client readiness, integrative eclecticism and the framework as a 'browser', ongoing evaluation through single-case thinking, and eight shadow-side pitfalls in the use of helping models.
objectives: Explain why Egan bases helping on a problem-management and opportunity-development framework.
List and explain the nine ingredients of successful therapy that the framework organises.
State Egan's four fundamental questions and map them onto the three stages and the action arrow.
Describe the three stages and nine tasks of the model, with the client question for each task.
Explain the role of implementation and the action arrow, and why the stages are planning for change.
Discuss the flexibility of the framework, including Kay's obliquity, entry points and Weick's dictum.
Describe Egan's thirteen stages of change and their link to client readiness for change.
Explain integrative eclecticism, pluralism and the framework as a 'browser'.
Explain how helpers can evaluate helping on an ongoing, case-by-case basis.
Critically discuss the shadow side of helping models.

sections.heading: Part III Opener: Why a Problem-Management and Opportunity-Development Approach?
sections.detailed:
Part III opens by explaining why Egan builds his whole approach around problem management. His argument is simple: whatever school a helper belongs to, every approach must in the end help clients manage problem situations and develop unused opportunities. It is therefore sensible to start with a framework that is flexible, humanistic and broadly based, one that deals directly with problems and opportunities.

Egan notes that writers on problem solving fall into two groups. Some name the process explicitly, such as Bedell and Lennox, Chang, D'Zurilla and Sanna, D'Zurilla and Nezu, Elias and Tobias, and Nezu and colleagues. Others use some version of the process without calling it problem solving, such as Bertolino and O'Hanlon, Cormier and Nurius, and Hill. General problem solving has about a century of research behind it; that the research is scattered does not reduce its importance. Egan cites Nobel laureate Herbert Simon and his associates, who argued that the work of managers, scientists, engineers and lawyers consists largely of making decisions and solving problems (choosing issues, setting goals, designing courses of action and choosing among alternatives) and that nothing matters more to society than doing this well at the national, organisational and individual levels.

Problem solving applied to individual lives goes by several names: social problem solving, applied problem solving, personal problem solving or human problem solving. It has a growing research base (Chang, D'Zurilla and Sanna; D'Zurilla and Nezu; Heppner, Witty and Dixon). Heppner's work focused on how people appraise their own ability to cope with personal problems. Confidence in one's problem-solving ability, the courage to face problems and a sense of self-control, especially emotional self-control, can lead to a richer life. O'Neil, commenting on this review, described helping others solve problems as a passionate part of the counselling psychologist's mission.

Egan then makes a social point. Parents agree that problem-management skills, like the communication skills of Part II, matter for their children, but they cannot say where children learn them: perhaps a little at home, perhaps at school. Yet school and college curricula contain little about solving problems in living. Some say such skills are simply picked up through experience, which is partly true. Egan's reply is that if these skills are so important, society should not leave them to chance; a problem-management mentality should be second nature, and the skills for learning in the "laboratory" of the world should be taught.

His conclusion is that the model of choice is a flexible, humanistic, broadly based problem-management and opportunity-development model that is straightforward without ignoring the complexity of clients' lives or of helping. Because this process is embedded in almost all approaches to helping, it gives a strong foundation for whatever "brand" of helping a trainee eventually chooses. The book provides the basics.
sections.simple: Every type of therapy ultimately has to help clients handle problems and use missed opportunities, so Egan starts from a flexible, humanistic problem-management model. Problem solving has about 100 years of research and is vital at personal and social levels. Egan argues these life skills should be taught rather than left to chance, and that this model is a foundation for any approach a helper later adopts.
keyPoints: All approaches must eventually help clients manage problems and develop unused opportunities.
Some writers name problem solving explicitly; others use the process without the name.
Herbert Simon: deciding and solving problems is central to work and to society.
Heppner: appraisal of one's ability to cope; confidence, courage and self-control lead to a richer life.
Schools rarely teach problem solving for problems in living; Egan says it should not be left to chance.
The model is embedded in nearly all approaches, so it is a foundation for any 'brand' of helping.

sections.heading: The Ingredients of Successful Therapy: A Review
sections.detailed:
At the start of Part III Egan revisits the ingredients of successful therapy introduced in Chapter 1. In Part III the problem-management and opportunity-development approach is presented as the organiser of these ingredients; they all sit, so to speak, inside this process.

1. The client and the contextual factors of the client's life. Clients and their needs are the centrepiece of problem-management helping. Keeping the client "in the driver's seat" remains one of the imperatives of therapy.

2. The person of the therapist. Parts I and II were about the therapist becoming competent in the skills needed to act as a consultant and catalyst in the client's efforts to manage problems and develop opportunities. But the therapist is not the main character; the client is.

3. The helping relationship. Client and therapist are not equal partners, because it is the client's problems, not the helper's, that are the focus. Instead they collaborate. Clients must manage their own problem situations, and therapists bring a tool kit that helps them do so. Helpers are successful only to the extent that clients are; the more they help clients bring out the best in themselves, the more successful they are.

4. The therapeutic dialogue between client and helper. Part II covered the communication skills helpers need, including using them to help clients communicate better. These skills are at the heart of the helper's role as consultant to the problem-management process.

5. Two-way feedback between client and helper. Following Duncan and colleagues, therapy is client-directed and outcome-informed. Feedback from session to session, on both progress towards outcomes and the usefulness of the sessions themselves, is critical.

6. The standard problem-management process as a human universal. The standard model is used directly or indirectly in almost every therapy, and in its basic form clients readily understand it.

7. The model or method of treatment and the assumptions behind it. The standard problem-management model is also a method of treatment in its own right. As presented in the book it is an experiential-cognitive-behavioural-emotive model covering the whole of human behaviour.

8. Decision making as a human universal. Decision making lies at the heart of problem management, since problems cannot be managed without decisions. Both helper and client need to understand how decision making works, including its ups and downs.

9. The beliefs, values, norms, ethics and morality that drive human behaviour. This package runs through all human behaviour. Because it is not "scientific" it makes every human transaction, therapy included, somewhat messy, but it too lies at the heart of therapy.

These themes run through Part III. Egan sums up the integrating process simply: the primary integrative process is a client successfully managing a problem situation.
sections.simple: Egan lists nine ingredients of successful therapy and says the problem-management process organises all of them. They are the client and context, the therapist, the relationship, the dialogue, two-way feedback, problem management as universal, the treatment model, decision making, and beliefs and values. What ties them together is a client successfully managing a problem.
keyPoints: The problem-management approach is the organiser of the ingredients of successful therapy.
The client is the centrepiece and stays 'in the driver's seat'; the therapist is not the main character.
Client and helper are not equal partners but collaborators; helpers succeed only as far as clients do.
Two-way feedback: therapy is client-directed and outcome-informed (Duncan and colleagues).
Problem management and decision making are human universals; the model is experiential-cognitive-behavioural-emotive.
The primary integrative process: a client successfully managing a problem situation.

sections.heading: Four Fundamental Questions and Figure 8.1
sections.detailed:
The chapter proper begins by recalling from Chapter 1 that every worthwhile helping framework ultimately helps clients ask and answer four basic questions for themselves.

1. What's going on? What problems, issues, concerns or undeveloped opportunities should I work on? This means helping clients spell out their current picture.

2. What does a better future look like? What do I want my life to look like, what changes would manage my problems and develop my opportunities, and what goals should I pursue? This means helping clients paint their preferred picture.

3. How do I get there? What must I do to make the preferred picture real, what plan will get me there, and what actions will start me on the right path? The plan sets out the actions needed for a better future; it is the way forward.

4. How do I make it all happen? How do I turn planning and goal setting into action that produces the results I want, and how do I get going and keep going until problems are managed and opportunities developed? This is the ongoing challenge of implementation.

In Figure 8.1 these four questions become three logical stages and an implementation arrow, the basic framework of helping. Stage I is the Current Picture (problems: my issues, concerns and unused opportunities). Stage II is the Preferred Picture (outcomes: what a better future looks like). Stage III is the Way Forward (plans: what I do to create that future). Underneath runs the Action arrow: how do I make it all happen?

Egan illustrates the value of an explicit problem-management focus with a study by Lagerveld and colleagues (2012). About 170 workers who had left work, usually temporarily, because of common mental health problems such as anxiety, depression, stress, adjustment disorder and emotional exhaustion were studied. Half received standard evidence-based CBT. The other half received a form of CBT that emphasised managing work-related problems and took a problem-management approach to returning to work. The work-focused group returned to work on average 65 days sooner.

Egan's interpretation is that both therapies probably had a problem-management focus, but the work-focused version was much more explicitly aimed at both relieving the disorder and getting back to work, and dealt more directly with the elements of Figure 8.1. It included Action-Arrow components: homework exercises, practising stress-reduction techniques, finding ways to change the work conditions that contributed to the problems, and an explicit return-to-work plan. The researchers were not trying to prove anything about problem management, but Egan argues that it is almost impossible to show anything about successful therapy without at least implicitly referring to elements of the process.
sections.simple: Every good helping framework helps clients answer four questions: what is going on, what would a better future look like, how do I get there, and how do I make it happen. Egan turns these into three stages (current picture, preferred picture, way forward) and an action arrow. In the Lagerveld study, workers given work-focused, problem-management CBT went back to work 65 days sooner than those given standard CBT.
keyPoints: Four questions: What's going on? What does a better future look like? How do I get there? How do I make it happen?
Figure 8.1: Stage I Current Picture, Stage II Preferred Picture, Stage III Way Forward, plus the Action arrow.
Lagerveld et al. (2012): about 170 workers off work with common mental health problems.
Work-focused CBT with a problem-management, return-to-work emphasis got people back 65 days sooner.
It used Action-Arrow elements: homework, stress reduction, changing work conditions, a return-to-work plan.

sections.heading: The Problem-Management Framework (Figure 8.2): Why 'Framework' Rather Than 'Model'
sections.detailed:
Figure 8.2 arranges the four elements in a more detailed and dynamic way. Stage I is "The Story" (What are my concerns?), Stage II is "Preferred Outcomes" (What do I need or want?) and Stage III is "A Practical Plan to Get Results" (How do I make it happen?). In the centre the helper's job is summed up as helping clients explore problems, set goals, devise plans and move to action, all resting on ongoing action leading to problem-managing outcomes. Similar graphics are used at each stage in later chapters.

Egan deliberately calls this a framework rather than a model, and gives his reasons:

- It organises all the ingredients of successful therapy outlined in Chapter 1.
- It lays out the "geography" of problem management, helping both client and therapist know where they are in the flow of helping.
- It is owned by both client and helper, so it promotes dialogue and collaboration.
- It has an ingrained logic and is systematic, but it is nonlinear. It is flexible with elastic borders: clients can move back and forth to the stages and tasks they find most useful, and therapists can invite clients into helpful areas they are overlooking.
- It is therefore both rigorous and soft-edged. It bends to the client's needs but stays focused on life-enhancing outcomes.

Egan says the theme of flexibility cannot be overstated, because many people reject the problem-management process as "rigid" and claim that ordinary people do not live their lives that way. He returns to this objection later in the chapter (see flexibility and obliquity). Later still (p. 231) he adds another reason for the word framework: it is an open-systems model, not a closed school.
sections.simple: Figure 8.2 shows the three stages (the story, preferred outcomes, a practical plan) sitting on ongoing action. Egan calls it a framework because it organises the ingredients of therapy, works like a map, is shared by client and helper, and is systematic but not linear. It is rigorous yet bends to the client's needs.
keyPoints: Figure 8.2: I The Story, II Preferred Outcomes, III A Practical Plan to Get Results, all on ongoing action.
Helper's role: help clients explore problems, set goals, devise plans and move to action.
Framework because it organises the ingredients of therapy and maps the 'geography' of helping.
Owned by both client and helper, so it fosters dialogue and collaboration.
Systematic but nonlinear, with elastic borders; both rigorous and soft-edged.
Answers the common complaint that problem management is 'rigid'.

sections.heading: Stage I: Help Clients Explore Their Concerns
sections.detailed:
Egan introduces the overview by saying each "stage" has three "tasks", sketched briefly here and treated in detail in later chapters. The overview is framed as questions clients can ask themselves.

In Stage I the tasks help clients spell out their concerns as clearly as possible, with neither too much nor too little detail. The three tasks help clients answer three sets of questions that outline the work they need to do, with the therapist's help, to move forward.

Task I-A. The Story: Problem Situations. "What's going on in my life? What are my main concerns?" Here the client tells their story and the helper helps them describe the problem situations and unused opportunities.

Task I-B. The Real Story: New Perspectives. "As I look more closely, what's really going on? What new perspectives will help me deal with my concerns?" The story as first told is rarely the whole story; this task helps the client see more deeply and from new angles.

Task I-C. The Right Story: Key Issues to Work On. "What should I be working on? Which issues, if handled well, will make a real difference in my life?" The client chooses the concerns that are worth working on and that will make a real difference.

Egan adds that the work done in any one of these tasks should stimulate actions that eventually lead to the client's preferred outcomes; exploration is not meant to be talk for its own sake.
sections.simple: Stage I helps clients get clear about what is wrong, with neither too much nor too little detail. Task A is telling the story, Task B is finding the real story through new perspectives, and Task C is choosing the right story, the key issues that will make a real difference. Even this exploring stage should lead to action.
keyPoints: Stage I aim: help clients spell out concerns clearly, with neither too much nor too little detail.
I-A The Story: 'What's going on in my life? What are my main concerns?'
I-B The Real Story (new perspectives): 'What's really going on?'
I-C The Right Story (key issues): 'Which issues, if handled well, will make a real difference?'
Work in any task should stimulate action towards preferred outcomes.

sections.heading: Stage II: Help Clients Determine Problem-Managing Outcomes and Set Goals
sections.detailed:
In Stage II therapists help clients imagine the kind of future they want, in terms of outcomes and goals. Its three interrelated tasks are three ways in which helpers can partner with clients to explore and develop this better future.

Task II-A. Possibilities. "What possibilities do I have for a better future? What do I want the future to look like? What do problem-managing outcomes look like?" The client is helped to imagine a range of possible better futures rather than settling for the first idea.

Task II-B. Goals/Outcomes. "What do I really want and need? What solutions are best for me?" From the possibilities the client chooses the goals that will actually manage the problem or develop the opportunity.

Task II-C. Commitment. "What am I willing to pay for what I want?" Goals cost something, and this task tests whether the client is committed enough to pay the price.

As with Stage I, Egan stresses that work on any of these tasks prompts actions that lead to the client's preferred outcomes. Note the shift: Stage I is about the current picture, while Stage II is about the preferred picture, the "what" of change rather than the "how".
sections.simple: Stage II helps clients picture the future they want. Task A brainstorms possibilities, Task B chooses the goals that really meet their needs, and Task C checks commitment by asking what they are willing to pay. This is the preferred picture.
keyPoints: Stage II aim: help clients imagine a better future in terms of outcomes and goals.
II-A Possibilities: 'What possibilities do I have for a better future?'
II-B Goals/Outcomes: 'What do I really want and need? What solutions are best for me?'
II-C Commitment: 'What am I willing to pay for what I want?'
Stage II is the 'preferred picture': what the client wants, not yet how to get it.

sections.heading: Stage III: Help Clients Draw Up Plans to Accomplish Goals
sections.detailed:
Stage III also has three interrelated tasks, aimed at producing a realistic plan to achieve the goals that lead to problem-managing outcomes.

Task III-A. Possible Strategies. "What are the possible paths to my goals? What kind of actions will help me get what I need and want? How do I move forward?" The client is helped to generate a range of possible routes.

Task III-B. Best-Fit Strategies. "What strategy or set of strategies is best for me? Which strategies fit my resources?" The client chooses strategies that suit their situation, resources and preferences.

Task III-C. Plans to Accomplish Goals. "What should my campaign for constructive change look like? How do I organise my strategies? What do I need to do first, second, third?" The chosen strategies are put into an ordered plan.

Egan closes the overview by noting that the stages, together with the tasks that make them work, form a logical process, but in practice not necessarily a linear, step-by-step one. He explains why later in the chapter under flexibility.
sections.simple: Stage III turns goals into a realistic plan. Task A brainstorms possible strategies, Task B picks the best-fit strategies for the client's resources, and Task C puts them into an ordered plan or 'campaign'. The stages are logical but not rigidly step-by-step.
keyPoints: Stage III aim: a realistic plan to reach the goals.
III-A Possible Strategies: 'What are the possible paths to my goals?'
III-B Best-Fit Strategies: 'Which strategies fit my resources?'
III-C Plans: 'What should my campaign for constructive change look like? What first, second, third?'
Stages and tasks are logical but not necessarily linear in practice.

sections.heading: Implementation: Help Clients Make It All Happen (the Action Arrow)
sections.detailed:
Implementation answers the client's question: how do I turn problem exploration, goal setting and planning into action that produces problem-managing and opportunity-developing results, and how do I get going and keep going until it happens? Egan's point is blunt: helping is about change, and change demands effort. Figure 8.3 highlights results-focused action.

All three stages sit on the "action arrow". This shows that clients need to act on their own behalf from the very beginning of helping, not only at the end. The arrow is a constant reminder that all three stages are about outcomes and the impact those outcomes have on clients' lives. The bias for action described in Chapter 2 must permeate every stage and every task.

Egan makes an important distinction. Stage I is about issues in the client's past and present that call for change. Stages II and III are about planning for change (setting goals and drawing up plans), not about constructive change itself. In fact all three stages and their nine tasks revolve around planning for change, not change itself. Talking about problems, discussing goals and working out strategies are just "blah, blah, blah" without goal-accomplishing action. Change does not emerge magically from therapy; it is hard work.

Yet every stage and task can promote action from the start. Egan stresses the need to build action into planning and planning into action, and later chapters note the "little actions" that get change moving at the very beginning of helping.

Figure 8.3 summarises three requirements for problem-managing action. It should start immediately, continue throughout the helping process, and lead to the client's preferred outcomes.

Counting the Action Arrow alongside the nine stage tasks gives the "ten tasks" or "moves" Egan refers to later in the chapter.
sections.simple: The action arrow runs under all three stages, meaning clients should act from the very first session. The three stages and nine tasks are only planning for change; without action it is all talk. Action should start immediately, continue throughout, and lead to the client's preferred outcomes.
keyPoints: Helping is about change, and change demands effort.
All three stages sit on the action arrow: clients act on their own behalf from the start.
Stages I-III and their nine tasks are planning for change, not change itself.
Without action, talk about problems, goals and strategies is 'blah, blah, blah'.
Figure 8.3: action should start immediately, continue throughout, and lead to preferred outcomes.
Build action into planning and planning into action; 'little actions' from the beginning.

sections.heading: Flexibility in the Use of the Problem-Management Process: Kay's Obliquity
sections.detailed:
Egan begins his discussion of flexibility with the British economist John Kay's book Obliquity (2011), which is broadly about problem management and opportunity development. Kay's thesis is that problem management, especially when it involves changing human behaviour, is best pursued indirectly rather than in a straight line.

Kay's reasoning runs as follows. We rarely know enough about the "moving parts" of important problems to tackle them head-on. Problem management evolves and is iterative. People are not very good at linear thinking, especially in messy situations, and emotions add to the confusion. An overly direct, linear change process blinds people to facts that contradict their assumptions. Logic and linearity can therefore get in the way of common sense and the best kind of intuition. Good solutions often emerge as we sift through possibilities, whereas logic and linearity can lock us into the solutions we prefer rather than those that work. Kay's advice is not to throw logic away but to use it with caution, and not to confuse logic with truth.

Egan applies this to his own framework. Because The Skilled Helper speaks of "stages" and "tasks", coded I, II, III and A, B, C, and adds the Action Arrow to make ten neatly packaged tasks, some readers may think change can be pursued in a prescriptive, linear fashion. There is a kind of linear logic to the process, but it should never be overstated: the logic is useful only to the extent that it serves clients' needs. Egan's summary is: don't be fooled by the logic, don't impose it on clients, and let clients' needs guide you.

So in later chapters the trainee learns ten different "tasks" or "moves", ten ways of helping clients move towards life-enhancing outcomes. The skill is to use these moves instinctively and wisely in the service of clients. Egan then sets out four specific points about flexibility: clients start and proceed differently; they engage in each stage and task differently; stages and tasks intermingle so clients move back and forth; and flexibility is not randomness or chaos.
sections.simple: John Kay's 'obliquity' says problems involving human behaviour are best tackled indirectly, because we rarely understand all their moving parts and too much linear logic blinds us. Egan applies this to his own model: the I-II-III and A-B-C labels have a logic, but it should never be imposed on clients. The ten tasks are 'moves' to be used flexibly and wisely for the client.
keyPoints: Kay (2011), Obliquity: problem management involving human behaviour is best pursued indirectly.
We rarely know the 'moving parts'; problem management is iterative; emotions add confusion.
Overly linear change blinds people to contradicting facts; use logic with caution; logic is not truth.
Nine stage tasks plus the Action Arrow = ten tasks or 'moves'.
Don't impose the model's logic on clients; let their needs guide you.
Use the moves instinctively and wisely in the service of clients.

sections.heading: Clients Start and Proceed Differently
sections.detailed:
The first point about flexibility is that any stage or task can be the entry point. Egan gives four clients:

- Client A starts with a strategy that failed. He threatened to quit unless given leave of absence, and it backfired: he was told to leave. The entry point is a failed strategy, which belongs to Stage III territory.
- Client B starts with what she wants but does not have: a boyfriend who will accept her as she is, because Joe keeps trying to change her. Her entry point is Stage II (wants and goals).
- Client C starts with the roots of his problem: he has never got over being abused by his uncle. His entry point is Stage I.
- Client D says she has no real problems but is vaguely dissatisfied; everyone says she has a great life, yet something is missing. The implication is that she has not been seizing opportunities that could make her happy. Here opportunity, not problem, is the starting point.

The lesson is that helpers must not insist that every client begin at Stage I, Task A. They need to recognise where a client has entered and work from there.
sections.simple: Clients can enter the helping process at any stage or task. One might begin with a failed strategy, another with what they want, another with the roots of a problem, and another with vague dissatisfaction that points to missed opportunities. The helper starts where the client starts.
keyPoints: Any stage or task can be the entry point.
Client A: a failed strategy (threatened to quit, was told to leave).
Client B: Stage II entry, what she wants but lacks (a partner who accepts her).
Client C: Stage I entry, roots of the problem (abuse by his uncle).
Client D: an opportunity, not a problem (great life but 'something's missing').

sections.heading: Clients Engage in Each Stage and Task Differently (Woody and Weick's Dictum)
sections.detailed:
The second point is that clients engage with each stage and task in their own way. Take storytelling: some clients pour out the whole story at once, some "leak" pieces of it throughout helping, and some tell only the parts that show them in a good light. Most talk about problems rather than opportunities.

Because clients rarely present all their problems at once in neat packages, it is impossible to complete Stage I before moving on to Stages II and III, and Egan says it is not even advisable. Some clients do not understand their problems until they start talking about what they want but do not have. Others need to take some remedial action before they can define the problem properly; in other words, action sometimes comes before understanding. If an attempted solution fails, the counsellor helps the client learn from it and return to clarifying the problem or opportunity and then setting realistic goals.

The case of Woody illustrates this. Woody, a college sophomore, came to student counselling with interpersonal and somatic complaints. He was attracted to several women on campus but did little about it. After a brief exploration he decided he simply had to go out and do it. Two months later he returned, calling his experiment a disaster. He had dated a few women but the "chemistry" never felt right. Then he met someone he liked, but on the third call she declined to see him again, vaguely saying he was too preoccupied with himself. Feeling miserable, he came back. This time he and the counsellor had real experiences to examine: the "chemistry thing" and his reaction to being called self-preoccupied.

Egan links Woody's case to Weick's (1979) dictum that chaotic action is sometimes preferable to orderly inactivity. Once Woody acted, he learned things about himself. Some lessons were painful, but he could now examine his interpersonal style much more concretely.
sections.simple: Clients tell their stories in different ways: all at once, in bits, or only the flattering parts. So Stage I can never be fully finished before moving on, and sometimes action comes before understanding. Woody's failed dating 'experiment' gave him real experiences to explore, showing Weick's idea that chaotic action can beat orderly inactivity.
keyPoints: Stories come all at once, leak out in pieces, or are told selectively; most clients talk about problems, not opportunities.
Stage I cannot, and should not, be completed before Stages II and III.
Some clients understand problems only by talking about what they want; action sometimes precedes understanding.
Failed actions are learning material; the helper helps the client return to clarifying and goal setting.
Woody: a failed dating 'experiment' gave concrete material on his interpersonal style.
Weick (1979): chaotic action is sometimes preferable to orderly inactivity.

sections.heading: Because the Stages and Tasks Intermingle, Clients Move Back and Forth
sections.simple: Stages and tasks often blend together, and new concerns can send the client back to exploring. In one short statement a client touched on a failed strategy, a questionable goal, a new problem, a relationship issue with the helper, a new approach and a new opportunity. The helper's job is to make sense of all this and guide the client to whatever stage helps most.
keyPoints: Tasks and even stages merge; one session can cover problem, goals and strategies.
New concerns during goal setting send the process back to exploration; helping is seldom linear.
Example client: failed strategy, questioned goal, new problem, helping-relationship issue, new approach, problem recast as opportunity.
Helper's challenge: make sense of entry points and guide clients through useful stages and tasks.

sections.heading: Flexibility Is Not Mere Randomness or Chaos
sections.detailed:
The fourth point balances the others. Focus and direction are also essential. Letting clients wander around in the mess of their problems in the name of flexibility leads nowhere.

The structure of the problem-management process is in fact the foundation for flexibility: it is the underlying "system" that keeps helping from becoming a set of random events. Returning to the geography metaphor, the stages and tasks are orientation devices. At its best the framework is a shared map that helps clients take a fuller part in helping, because they too need to know where they are going.

So Egan's position is neither rigid nor structureless. The structure gives direction; flexibility lets the helper respond to each client's needs and entry point.
sections.simple: Flexibility does not mean letting clients drift aimlessly. The structure of the model is what makes flexibility possible, acting like a map that both helper and client use. Clients also need to know where they are heading.
keyPoints: Focus and direction are essential; wandering in the name of flexibility leads nowhere.
Structure is the foundation for flexibility, the 'system' that prevents randomness.
Stages and tasks are orientation devices (geography metaphor).
The framework is a shared map that helps clients participate more fully.

sections.heading: Stages of Change and Client Readiness for Change: The Source Models
sections.detailed:
Egan notes that the problem-management process can also be described in terms of the natural stages of change and what clients think, feel and do at each stage.

He draws on two models. Yankelovich (1992) offered a seven-step process. Prochaska and colleagues (Norcross, Krebs and Prochaska; Prochaska and DiClemente; Prochaska and Norcross), seeing helping as facilitating client change, developed a five-stage process covering both client-mediated and helper-assisted change, which many helpers find useful. The five stages are precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance.

Both models are forms of the problem-management process, and both offer insight into a client's readiness for change. Egan then presents his own reworked combination of the two as a thirteen-step sequence: unawareness, initial awareness, heightened awareness, preliminary actions, urgency, search for remedies, estimation of costs, weighing the costs, rational decision, rational-emotional decision, serious action, maintenance and relapse. These are covered in the next three sections.
sections.simple: Egan links problem management to the natural stages people go through when they change. He combines Yankelovich's seven steps with Prochaska's five stages (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance) into his own 13-step sequence. Both models help a helper judge how ready a client is to change.
keyPoints: Problem management can be described through natural stages of change.
Yankelovich (1992): a seven-step process.
Prochaska and colleagues: five stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance.
Both models are forms of problem management and shed light on readiness for change.
Egan reworks and combines them into 13 steps, from unawareness to relapse.

sections.heading: Stages of Change 1-5: From Unawareness to Urgency
sections.detailed:
1. Unawareness. The person is unaware of having a problem, only vaguely aware, or aware but with no intention of doing anything. Sunil tells neighbours who complain about late-night noise from him and his flatmates that it is their problem, not his, and they should take sleeping pills. Clarissa's friends warn her about her health given her heart condition. Resistance to recognising or dealing with a problem is the hallmark of this stage. There is no readiness for change.

2. Initial awareness. Clients become aware of an issue, but readiness for change is still very low. After repeated disputes over household finances, a couple develop a vague sense of dissatisfaction with the relationship itself. Clive has two DUI (drink-driving) citations; a third means mandatory jail. He is vaguely aware of the legal consequences, the thought pops up now and then, and he even drinks a little less when he has to drive. But he is still unaware that he is a problem drinker.

3. Heightened awareness. The person knows there is a problem and thinks seriously about acting but has not committed to action. William says he knows smoking is ruining him and he must give it up sooner or later. He is still ambivalent. The price of change still seems too high, but the person has moved beyond mere awareness to significant consideration of change. Serious motivation is still missing.

4. Preliminary actions. The person is on the verge of doing something or has already tried, however unsuccessfully. The actions are often feeble or symbolic. William proudly reports he is down to eight cigarettes a day from two packs. People here may try to avoid temptation and do some planning, however meagre.

5. Urgency. A sense of urgency develops, especially as the problem becomes more distressing. A married couple's dissatisfaction grows so that even small annoyances are seen through overall dissatisfaction. Clive is stopped for an illegal turn; the officer checks his record and breathalyses him although he has not been drinking. The incident shakes him; he realises he came very close to jail and finally has a heightened awareness that he is a problem drinker.

Note how the early stages map loosely onto Prochaska's precontemplation (unawareness), contemplation (initial and heightened awareness) and preparation (preliminary actions).
sections.simple: In the first five steps the person moves from denying the problem (unawareness), to vaguely noticing it (initial awareness), to seriously thinking about it while still ambivalent (heightened awareness), to small symbolic actions (preliminary actions), and finally to feeling it must be dealt with (urgency). Egan illustrates these with Sunil, Clive, William and a married couple.
keyPoints: 1 Unawareness: denial or no intention to act; resistance is the hallmark (Sunil).
2 Initial awareness: vague awareness, very low readiness (Clive's DUIs; couple's finance disputes).
3 Heightened awareness: knows the problem, ambivalent, change seems too costly (William on smoking).
4 Preliminary actions: feeble or symbolic steps (William down to eight cigarettes).
5 Urgency: distress grows; a shock brings it home (Clive breathalysed).

sections.heading: Stages of Change 6-10: From Search for Remedies to Rational-Emotional Decision
sections.detailed:
6. Search for remedies. Clients begin to look for remedies and, however implicitly or half-heartedly, explore strategies. People in difficult marriages think about complaining openly to partners or friends, separating, divorcing, small acts of revenge, having an affair, seeing a marriage counsellor or a minister, or withdrawing from the relationship. They may try one or more of these without evaluating cost or consequences.

7. Estimation of costs. The costs of the different remedies become apparent. Someone in a troubled relationship may realise that openness has not worked and continuing it will mean confrontation, denial, argument and counter-accusations; or that withdrawing has been painful, and wonder what living alone would mean or what would happen to the children. At this point clients often back away from dealing with the problem directly, because there is no cost-free, painless option.

8. Weighing the costs. Because the problem does not go away, complete retreat is impossible, so a more serious weighing of choices begins, for example the costs of confronting the situation against the costs of withdrawing. Often an inner dialogue moves back and forth between steps 7 and 8, as in a person concluding that a painful separation might be worth it for the children's sake.

9. Rational decision. An intellectual decision is made to accept a choice and pursue a course of action, such as raising everything with one's spouse and suggesting marriage counselling, or getting on with life and letting the marriage go where it will.

10. Rational-emotional decision. A purely intellectual decision is often not enough to drive action, so the heart joins the head. One spouse declares they have had enough and are leaving, uncomfortable as it will be; the other decides that going on like this is unfair to both and bad for the children, and this drives the decision to seek help even alone. Egan's key point: decisions driven by conviction and emotion are more likely to be turned into action.
sections.simple: Next the person starts looking for remedies, then sees what each will cost and often backs off, then seriously weighs the costs because the problem will not go away. A rational decision follows, but action really happens when emotion joins it in a rational-emotional decision.
keyPoints: 6 Search for remedies: strategies are tried, often without weighing cost or consequences.
7 Estimation of costs: no painless option, so clients often back away.
8 Weighing the costs: retreat is impossible; serious comparison; inner dialogue between 7 and 8.
9 Rational decision: an intellectual choice of a course of action.
10 Rational-emotional decision: heart joins head; conviction plus emotion drives action.

sections.heading: Stages of Change 11-13: Serious Action, Maintenance and Relapse
sections.detailed:
11. Serious action. People are now engaged in life-enhancing change and put real time and effort into modifying dysfunctional behaviour. Change is visible and recognised by others. The hallmark of this stage is modifying the undesirable behaviour to an acceptable standard through systematic effort.

12. Maintenance. The person consolidates gains and works to avoid relapse. This can last a long time, even a lifetime, as for someone who fights the urge to smoke every day. A married couple might keep looking for ways to "reinvent" their marriage. Clive stops drinking and joins Alcoholics Anonymous, attending a meeting every day to stay dry.

13. Relapse. People are prone to relapse. Egan distinguishes a minor lapse, a relapse and a total collapse into the old ways. Clive goes out with friends who mock his AA membership, gets drunk, and is taken home. People can learn from lapses: the next morning Clive realises how foolish it was to think he could go out with drinking companions and not drink. A relapse or total collapse can mean moving back to an earlier stage or starting the whole process again. Clive cannot afford that, and returns to AA.

Egan ends with a caution. Keeping this process in mind helps helpers meet clients "where they are" and tailor the problem-management process to their needs. But it is a conceptual framework to help work with clients; becoming preoccupied with any framework is a disservice to clients.
sections.simple: In serious action the person puts in real, visible, systematic effort to change. Maintenance means holding on to gains and avoiding relapse, sometimes for life. Relapse can be a small lapse or a total collapse, and people can learn from it. The stages help helpers meet clients where they are, but should not become an obsession.
keyPoints: 11 Serious action: visible, systematic effort to modify dysfunctional behaviour.
12 Maintenance: consolidating gains and avoiding relapse, possibly for a lifetime (Clive joins AA).
13 Relapse: lapse vs relapse vs total collapse; lapses can teach; may mean going back a stage or restarting.
Use the stages to meet clients 'where they are'.
Preoccupation with any framework is a disservice to clients.

sections.heading: Integrative Eclecticism: The Ongoing Search for Best Practice
sections.detailed:
Egan observes that every form of therapy deals with clients' experiences, cognitions, internal and external behaviour and emotions. In that sense every therapy is a cognitive-behavioural-emotive approach, and that is certainly true of the problem-management process. It is both a process inherent in every form of therapy and a valid approach to treatment in its own right.

Even so, no single approach will ever be the "last word" in helping, for at least two and perhaps three reasons:

1. Ongoing research into human behaviour and helping will always either challenge cherished ideas about clients and therapy or complement ideas that have stood the test of time.
2. Effective helpers will always be looking for better ways to deliver their services.
3. Clients will always expect, knowingly or not, best practice from their helpers.

This sets up the idea of integrative eclecticism: a continual, systematic search for what works best for clients, discussed in the next two sections.
sections.simple: Every therapy deals with experiences, thoughts, behaviour and emotions, so in a sense all are cognitive-behavioural-emotive, including problem management. But no approach will ever be the final word, because research keeps moving, good helpers keep looking for better methods, and clients expect best practice.
keyPoints: Every therapy deals with experience, cognition, behaviour and emotion: all are cognitive-behavioural-emotive.
Problem management is inherent in every therapy and a valid treatment in itself.
No approach is the 'last word': research challenges or complements ideas.
Effective helpers keep seeking better ways to deliver services.
Clients expect best practice, knowingly or not.

sections.heading: Client-Focused Eclecticism and Integration
sections.detailed:
Many experienced helpers, even when committed to one school, borrow methods and techniques from other approaches. Some, without declaring allegiance to any school, stitch together their own approach. This borrowing and stitching is called eclecticism (Corey; Jensen, Bergin and Greaves; Lazarus, Beutler and Norcross; Norcross and Goldfried; Prochaska and Norcross). In one study about 40% of helpers said eclecticism was their primary approach (Milan, Montgomery and Rogers, 1994).

Effective eclecticism, however, must be more than random borrowing of ideas and techniques. There must be an integrating framework that gives the whole process coherence; to be effective, eclecticism must be systematic (Corey; Norcross and Goldfried).

Cooper and McLeod (2011) see their "pluralistic" approach as going a step beyond integrative eclecticism. Pluralistic practice rests on the pluralistic perspective: the belief that different clients are likely to benefit from different things at different times, and that therapists should work closely with clients to identify what they want from therapy and how they might get it. Practice therefore centres on dialogue between client and helper to identify goals, tasks and methods drawn from many therapeutic orientations. Keeping the client in the driver's seat is central. Their integrating framework consists of three overlapping domains: goals, tasks and methods of therapy, which Egan notes are terms at the heart of problem management.

Egan concludes that Cooper and McLeod, Duncan and colleagues, and Egan himself "all sit in the same church, but perhaps in different pews": they share the same basic commitments while differing in emphasis.
sections.simple: Many helpers borrow techniques from different schools; this is eclecticism, and about 40% of helpers in one study said it was their main approach. To work, eclecticism must be systematic, held together by an integrating framework. Cooper and McLeod's pluralistic approach, built on dialogue about goals, tasks and methods, is close to Egan's own view.
keyPoints: Eclecticism: borrowing and stitching together methods from different approaches.
Milan, Montgomery and Rogers (1994): about 40% of helpers named eclecticism as their primary approach.
Effective eclecticism must be systematic, held together by an integrating framework.
Cooper and McLeod (2011): pluralistic perspective; different clients benefit from different things at different times.
Pluralistic framework: goals, tasks and methods, decided in dialogue with the client in the driver's seat.
Cooper and McLeod, Duncan and Egan: 'same church, different pews'.

sections.heading: The Problem-Management Framework as 'Browser'
sections.detailed:
How do helpers borrow from many approaches and stitch them together? Egan proposes that the problem-management process can act as a tool, a "browser" in internet terms, for mining, organising and evaluating concepts and techniques that work for clients, whatever their origin. The functions are:

1. Mining. Helpers can use the model to mine any school or approach, digging out what is useful without accepting everything it offers. The model's philosophy, communication skills, stages and tasks are tools for identifying methods that serve clients.

2. Organising. Because the model is organised by stages and tasks, it can organise the methods mined from the helping literature. For example, many contemporary therapies offer excellent techniques for identifying blind spots and developing new perspectives; in Chapters 6 and 7 these were organised around those two concepts.

3. Evaluating. Because the model is pragmatic and outcome-focused, it can be used to evaluate the huge number of techniques constantly being devised. The helper asks how a technique contributes to the "bottom line": outcomes that serve clients' needs.

4. Incorporating. The best ideas can be incorporated into the helper's ever-evolving framework, replacing outdated ideas, correcting flawed ones and enhancing viable ones. Egan says every edition of his book has done exactly this, and he is puzzled when people ask why a new edition is needed.

5. The client as decision maker. Duncan and colleagues, Cooper and McLeod, and Egan all insist that the client is the decision maker and must be intimately involved in every decision. Egan perhaps goes further by "nudging" clients and inviting them to self-challenge (Chapter 6). Some might call this "fudging", but he sees it as an essential service.

The model can serve these functions because it is an open-systems model, not a closed school, which is why Egan now calls it a framework. It takes a stand on how helpers may help, but it is open to being corroborated, complemented and challenged by any other approach. The needs of clients, not the egos of model builders, must stay central; clients deserve best practice whatever its source.
sections.simple: Egan says his framework can work like a 'browser': it helps helpers mine useful techniques from any school, organise them by stage and task, evaluate them by their results, and incorporate the best into their own practice. The client remains the decision maker. Because it is an open system rather than a closed school, Egan calls it a framework.
keyPoints: Mining: dig out what is useful from any approach without accepting everything.
Organising: arrange techniques by stages and tasks (e.g. blind spots, new perspectives).
Evaluating: judge techniques by their contribution to client outcomes, the 'bottom line'.
Incorporating: replace outdated ideas, correct flawed ones, enhance viable ones.
Client as decision maker; Egan adds 'nudging' and invitations to self-challenge.
Open-systems model, not a closed school; client needs, not model builders' egos, come first.

sections.heading: 'How Are We Doing?': Ongoing Evaluation of the Helping Process
sections.detailed:
Given the importance of feedback discussed in Chapter 1, how do helpers using this framework evaluate what is happening with each client? Egan's answer is to make each case a "mini-experiment".

Psychological research has a long history of N = 1, or single-case, research designs used both to evaluate practice and to do research (Blampied; Borckardt and colleagues; Elliott; Hilliard; Kazdin; Lundervold and Belwood; Sharpley). It is not enough to know that helping works in general; helpers need to know how well it is working in each case. Jay Lebow (2002) observes that any clinician can use the single-case design with any client, and that it is simply a more formal, systematic way of documenting what the clinician does anyway. He, like Duncan, recommends questionnaires to document changes both in therapy and in the client's daily life. Bangert and Baumberger (2005) argue that although N = 1 is the most relevant design for practising counsellors, few are skilled at using it.

In many helping models evaluation is presented as the last step. Egan argues that evaluation only at the end is too late. Mash and Hunsley (1993) noted that early detection of what is going wrong is needed to prevent failure, and claimed that an early-detection framework should be theory-based, ongoing, practical, and sensitive to new perspectives that emerge during helping.

Egan says the problem-management and opportunity-development framework meets these requirements. It is a tool for checking progress throughout helping, and it provides criteria for helper effectiveness, client participation and assessing outcomes. Evaluation is therefore built into every stage rather than tacked on at the end.
sections.simple: Egan wants every case treated as a small experiment, using single-case (N = 1) methods to check how well helping is working for that particular client. Evaluation should happen all through helping, not just at the end, so problems are caught early. His framework provides criteria for judging helper effectiveness, client participation and outcomes.
keyPoints: Each case is a 'mini-experiment'; N = 1 single-case designs evaluate practice.
Need to know how well helping works in each case, not just in general.
Lebow (2002): single-case design is a systematic way of documenting what clinicians already do; use questionnaires.
Bangert and Baumberger (2005): N = 1 is most relevant, but few counsellors are adept at it.
Mash and Hunsley (1993): early detection needs a framework that is theory-based, ongoing, practical and sensitive.
The framework gives criteria for helper effectiveness, client participation and outcomes.

sections.heading: Understanding and Dealing with the Shadow Side of Helping Models
sections.detailed:
Egan acknowledges an obvious objection. His book presents a helping framework that is rational, linear and systematic, but the world is often irrational, nonlinear and chaotic, so what good is it?

His answer is that rational frameworks help clients bring much-needed discipline and order into chaotic lives, especially when the frameworks are culturally flexible. Effective helpers do not apologise for using such frameworks, but they make sure their own humanity permeates them.

Besides the broad shadow-side themes raised earlier in the book, Egan lists specific shadow-side pitfalls in the use of any helping model: having no model or framework; confusing and needless multiplication of helping models; fads and forgetfulness; failure to share the helping model; rigid application of treatment methods; chaos in defining competence; failure to grow with the profession; and the ethics involved in training helpers. Each is discussed in the sections that follow.
sections.simple: A rational, systematic model might seem out of place in a chaotic world, but Egan says such frameworks help clients bring order to messy lives, especially when they are culturally flexible and applied with humanity. He then lists eight specific shadow-side pitfalls in using helping models.
keyPoints: Objection: a rational, linear framework in an irrational, chaotic world.
Answer: rational frameworks bring discipline and order to clients' chaotic lives.
Frameworks should be culturally flexible and permeated by the helper's humanity.
Eight pitfalls: no model, multiplication of models, fads and forgetfulness, failure to share, rigidity, competence chaos, failure to grow, training ethics.

sections.heading: No Model or Framework
sections.detailed:
Some helpers simply "wing it". They have no consistent, integrated model of treatment that they have made their own. Some use a version of the problem-management process without realising that is what they are doing.

Professional training programmes often present a wide range of approaches drawn from the "major brands". If trainees leave knowing a lot about different approaches but without an integrated approach of their own, they need to develop one quickly. Egan suggests the problem-management and opportunity-development framework as a good starting point, because it is inevitably at the core of other helping models.

He adds a research-based reminder: helpers need a method of treatment that they believe in, that they are competent in, and that they share with clients.
sections.simple: Some helpers 'wing it' with no consistent model of their own, or use problem management without knowing it. Trainees who learn many approaches but have no integrated one should build one fast, and problem management is a good start. Research says helpers need a method they believe in, are competent in, and share with clients.
keyPoints: Some helpers 'wing it' without a consistent, integrated model.
Some use problem management unknowingly.
Trainees exposed to many 'brands' must quickly develop their own integrated approach.
Problem management is a good start because it is at the core of other models.
Helpers need a method they believe in, are competent in, and share with clients.

sections.heading: Confusing and Needless Multiplication of Helping Models
sections.detailed:
A computer search reveals dozens, if not hundreds, of methods, treatments and approaches, all claiming high success. Egan accepts that helpers must understand the disorders they are helping clients manage, but he regards multiple models for almost every known psychological disorder as "a thought too far".

Likewise, understanding the developmental tasks and challenges of different age groups matters, but having a separate model of therapy for each age group, and sometimes for subgroups from childhood to old age, is in his word a "stretch". Add approaches built around terms such as emotions, mindfulness, motivation and strengths, and it is no surprise the number runs into the hundreds.

Egan is careful to say he is not claiming these authors have nothing of value; far from it. His point is that the profession needs a better way of distilling and organising its research findings and clinical wisdom, which links back to using the problem-management framework as an organiser and "browser".
sections.simple: There are hundreds of therapy models, each claiming success, with models for nearly every disorder, age group and popular concept. Egan says many contain value, but the profession needs a better way to distil and organise its research and clinical wisdom instead of multiplying models.
keyPoints: Dozens or hundreds of approaches, all claiming high success.
Multiple models for almost every disorder is 'a thought too far'.
A separate model for each age group and subgroup is a 'stretch'.
Models also built around emotions, mindfulness, motivation, strengths and the like.
These authors offer value, but the profession needs better ways to distil and organise knowledge.

sections.heading: Fads and Forgetfulness
sections.detailed:
The helping professions are not immune to fads. Egan defines a fad as an insight or technique that would have some merit if integrated into an overall model or framework, but which is instead marketed on its own as the central, if not the only meaningful, intervention. A fad need not be new; it can be the "rediscovery" of a truth or technique that has never found its proper place in the helping tool kit.

He quotes Rachman (2008), who compares the market for ideas to the share market: it always overshoots. Ideas become fashionable and are pushed to and beyond their logical conclusions as backers give in to "irrational exuberance", and then comes the crash. Helpers fall in love with such ideas for a while and then abandon them. Egan's advice: there will always be "hot topics"; note them and integrate whatever is useful into a comprehensive approach. Proponents of many new approaches make outrageous claims. Do not ignore them, but take the claims with a grain of salt and test the approach.

The opposite problem is "irrational forgetfulness". Really good ideas are highlighted for a while and then shoved into a drawer instead of being developed and incorporated into practice. Egan's examples: there is little talk today about the "laws of human behaviour" (Watson and Tharp, 2007) based on incentives, rewards and punishment, and "cognitive dissonance" is seldom heard, though a popular book (Tarves and Aronson, 2007) has recently revived it.
sections.simple: A fad is a useful idea or technique marketed as the one key answer instead of being fitted into a wider framework; it may even be an old idea 'rediscovered'. Rachman compares this to a share market that overshoots and crashes. The opposite problem, irrational forgetfulness, is when good ideas such as the laws of behaviour or cognitive dissonance are dropped.
keyPoints: Fad: an insight with some merit, marketed alone as the central or only intervention instead of being integrated.
A fad can be a 'rediscovery' of an old truth or technique.
Rachman (2008): the market for ideas overshoots, then crashes.
Advice: integrate useful hot topics; take outrageous claims with a grain of salt and test them.
Irrational forgetfulness: good ideas shelved, e.g. laws of human behaviour (Watson and Tharp), cognitive dissonance (Tarves and Aronson).

sections.heading: Failure to Share the Helping Model
sections.detailed:
Some counsellors are reluctant to tell clients what the helping process is about. Those who "fly by the seat of their pants" cannot explain it, because they do not know what it is about themselves. Others seem to think knowledge of helping processes is secret, sacred or dangerous and should not be shared with clients, although there is no evidence for such beliefs (Duncan and colleagues, 2010).

Egan's counter-argument follows from the client-in-the-driver's-seat principle: if the client is to be in charge, they need a basic grasp of the helping process and should be encouraged to make decisions about it and within it. This links to the earlier point that the framework is owned by both client and helper and works as a shared map.
sections.simple: Some counsellors do not explain the helping process to clients, either because they have no clear model or because they think it should be kept secret, though there is no evidence for that. If clients are to be in the driver's seat, they need to understand the process and make decisions within it.
keyPoints: Helpers who 'fly by the seat of their pants' can't share a model they don't have.
Some think helping knowledge is secret, sacred or dangerous; no evidence supports this (Duncan et al., 2010).
Clients in the driver's seat need a basic grasp of the process.
Clients should be encouraged to make decisions about and within the framework.

sections.heading: Rigid Applications of Treatment Methods
sections.detailed:
Some helpers adopt a model early and then ignore later challenges to it or changes in it. They stop being learners, and the "purity" of the model becomes more important than clients' needs.

Other helpers, especially beginners, apply a useful model too rigidly, dragging clients through it in a linear way even when that is not what the clients need.

Egan says both add up to excessive control. His principle is that effective models, used effectively, are liberating rather than controlling. This echoes the earlier discussion of Kay's obliquity and the warning not to impose the logic of the stages on clients.
sections.simple: Some helpers stick to a model they learned early and ignore new developments, valuing its 'purity' over clients. Beginners may march clients through a model step by step whether it helps or not. Both are too controlling; good models used well should free clients, not control them.
keyPoints: Some helpers stop learning; the model's 'purity' matters more than clients' needs.
Beginners may drag clients linearly through a model.
Both amount to excessive control.
Effective models effectively used are liberating rather than controlling.

sections.heading: Chaos in Defining Competence
sections.detailed:
Chapters 1 and 2 gave a short, evidence-based picture of the competent helper. The professional "long form" looks very different. A Special Section of seven highly academic articles in Professional Psychology: Research and Practice (2007) set out the ambition of a "cradle to grave" assessment system covering all helping competencies, including knowledge, skills, dispositions, self-perceptions, motives and beliefs-attitudes (Kaslow and associates, 2007).

Egan finds that these articles at times present helping almost as an adjunct to medicine. But assessing the competence of a gall-bladder surgeon is quite different from assessing a marriage counsellor. The 15 guiding principles for assessing competence are, he says, brutally thorough and highly academic.

Lichtenberg and colleagues (2007) outlined the challenges of picturing the competent helper and concluded that reaching consensus across the profession's specialties, orientations and models on necessary competencies is a critical first step. Egan's verdict is that the profession is still at the starting gate. There is broad agreement that helping generally helps and that a set of "common factors" contributes to success, but practitioners are divided about what competence in helping actually is.
sections.simple: The profession has tried to build a detailed 'cradle to grave' system for assessing helper competence, with 15 guiding principles, but Egan finds it overly academic and too medical. Lichtenberg says agreement on competencies is a necessary first step. There is broad agreement that helping works and that common factors matter, but no agreement on what competence is.
keyPoints: Professional Psychology: Research and Practice (2007) special section: seven articles on competence assessment.
Kaslow and associates: 'cradle to grave' assessment of knowledge, skills, dispositions, self-perceptions, motives, beliefs-attitudes.
Helping treated almost as an adjunct to medicine; a surgeon differs from a marriage counsellor.
15 guiding principles: brutally thorough and highly academic.
Lichtenberg et al.: consensus on competencies is a critical first step; the profession is 'still at the starting gate'.

sections.heading: Failure to Grow with the Profession
sections.detailed:
Egan recalls his first talk to a group of experienced helpers, who turned out to know little about current research in the helping professions. He was surprised, even a bit shocked, though he admits they may have been very successful and his reaction may reflect his being an "academic twit". Still, he expected helpers who wanted to increase their competence to keep up with relevant theory and practice research, and this does not seem to happen.

Boisvert and Faust (2006), in a study of over 180 practitioners, found a disconnect between what practitioners think research says and what it actually says. Many practitioners consider much, if not most, research irrelevant to their practice.

Another study made Egan reflect. Cook and colleagues (2009) found that the biggest influences on therapists' willingness to learn a new treatment were whether it could be integrated with the therapy they already provided and whether therapists they respected endorsed it. Clinicians were more willing to keep using a new treatment when they could deliver it effectively and enjoyably and when clients liked it and reported improvement. Egan concludes that many practitioners may look sceptically at the flood of research and take a more common-sense approach.
sections.simple: Many experienced helpers do not keep up with research, and Boisvert and Faust found practitioners often misunderstand what research says and think it irrelevant. Cook and colleagues found therapists adopt a new treatment when it fits what they already do and respected colleagues endorse it, and keep using it when it works and clients like it.
keyPoints: Egan found experienced helpers knew little about current research.
Boisvert and Faust (2006), 180+ practitioners: gap between what they think research says and what it says; much seen as irrelevant.
Cook et al. (2009): willingness to learn a new treatment depends on integration with current therapy and endorsement by respected therapists.
Continued use depends on effective, enjoyable delivery and clients liking it and improving.
Practitioners may be sceptical of the research flood and take a common-sense approach.

sections.heading: The Ethics Involved in the Training of Helpers
sections.detailed:
Finally, and no less important, Egan raises ethical issues in training helpers. Barnett (2008), as editor of a Focus on Ethics section of Professional Psychology: Research and Practice, oversaw three short articles on this "hot potato".

Not everyone accepted into a doctoral programme turns out well. Some trainees do not reach basic competence. Some are high academic achievers yet lack even initial professional competence. Some arrive with, or develop, behavioural problems or disorders that prevent them from being effective. Some fail the ethical behaviour test.

Egan has seen the "hot potato" first-hand. Years ago these issues were often ignored. In today's climate of accountability they are harder (though not impossible) to ignore, so responsibility is passed around, and some people who should never be helpers slip through the cracks. The articles in Barnett's section suggest systemic ways of managing the problem. Egan hopes it will be managed better but, like many human problems, never fully solved. Better selection of candidates is the starting point, though selection brings its own difficulties: false positives and false negatives at the start, and possible lawsuits in the middle and at the end of training.
sections.simple: Some trainees never become competent, lack professional skills despite good grades, have behavioural problems, or fail on ethics. Responsibility for dealing with them is often passed around like a 'hot potato', so unsuitable people become helpers. Better selection is the starting point, though it brings false positives, false negatives and lawsuits.
keyPoints: Barnett (2008) edited three articles on this 'hot potato' issue.
Problem trainees: lack basic competence; academically strong but professionally weak; behavioural problems or disorders; fail the ethics test.
Once ignored; now responsibility is shuttled around and some slip through the cracks.
Systemic solutions suggested; the problem will be managed better but never fully solved.
Better selection is the starting point, despite false positives and negatives and possible lawsuits.

terms.definition: Egan's flexible, humanistic, broadly based helping framework that helps clients manage problem situations and develop unused opportunities; embedded in almost all approaches to helping.
Problem solving applied at the level of individual lives; it has an evolving research base.

Nine factors (client and context, therapist, relationship, dialogue, two-way feedback, problem management as universal, treatment model, decision making, beliefs and values) organised by the problem-management process.
Duncan and colleagues' description of therapy in which session-to-session feedback on progress and on the usefulness of sessions is critical.
Stage I answer to 'What's going on?': the problems, issues, concerns and unused opportunities the client should work on.
Stage II answer to 'What does a better future look like?': the changes and goals the client wants.
Stage III answer to 'How do I get there?': the plan of actions needed to create a better future.
The arrow beneath all three stages showing that clients must act on their own behalf from the start; the ongoing challenge of implementation.
Egan's preferred term for his process: it organises the ingredients of therapy, maps the geography of helping, is shared by client and helper, and is systematic but nonlinear.
Helping clients describe problem situations: 'What's going on in my life? What are my main concerns?'
Helping clients develop new perspectives: 'What's really going on?'
Helping clients choose key issues that, if handled well, will make a real difference.
Exploring possibilities for a better future and what problem-managing outcomes look like.
Choosing what the client really wants and needs: the solutions best for them.
'What am I willing to pay for what I want?'
Identifying the possible paths and actions that could lead to the client's goals.
Choosing the strategy or set of strategies that best suits the client and fits their resources.
Organising strategies into a sequenced 'campaign for constructive change'.
Turning exploration, goal setting and planning into action that produces results, and persevering until change happens.
John Kay's thesis that problem management, especially changing human behaviour, is best pursued indirectly rather than linearly.
The nine stage tasks plus the Action Arrow: ten ways of helping clients move towards life-enhancing outcomes, to be used flexibly.
The stage or task at which a client begins the helping process; any stage or task can be the entry point.
Chaotic action is sometimes preferable to orderly inactivity.
The stages and tasks seen as a shared map that tells helper and client where they are and where they are going.
Prochaska and colleagues' five stages of client-mediated and helper-assisted change.
Egan's first stage of change: unaware, vaguely aware, or aware with no intention to act; resistance is its hallmark; no readiness.
Becoming aware of an issue while readiness for change remains very low.
Knowing there is a problem and seriously considering change, but ambivalent and not yet committed.
Being on the verge of acting or making feeble, symbolic attempts at change.
A growing sense that the problem must be dealt with as it becomes more distressing.
Exploring and trying strategies, often without evaluating cost or consequences.
Seeing the costs of remedies; clients often back away because no option is painless.
Seriously comparing the costs of different choices because the problem will not go away.
An intellectual decision to pursue a course of action.
A decision in which the heart joins the head; conviction and emotion make action more likely.
Visible, systematic effort to modify dysfunctional behaviour to an acceptable standard.
Consolidating gains and working to avoid relapse; may last a lifetime.
Falling back; Egan distinguishes a minor lapse, a relapse and a total collapse into old ways.
Borrowing methods from different approaches, or stitching together one's own approach without allegiance to a school.
Eclecticism held together by an integrating framework that gives the process coherence, rather than random borrowing.
Cooper and McLeod's belief that different clients benefit from different things at different times, with therapist and client working out together what is wanted and how to get it.
Using the framework to mine, organise, evaluate and incorporate concepts and techniques from any source.
A framework that takes a stand yet is open to being corroborated, complemented and challenged by other approaches; the reason Egan calls his a framework.
Research design that treats each case as a mini-experiment to evaluate practice with an individual client.
Mash and Hunsley: a framework for spotting what is going wrong early; should be theory-based, ongoing, practical and sensitive to new perspectives.
Helping without a consistent, integrated model of one's own.
An insight or technique with some merit that is marketed on its own as the central or only intervention instead of being integrated into a wider framework.
Highlighting good ideas for a while and then shelving them rather than developing and incorporating them.
Egan's label for unsuitable trainees whose problems get passed around rather than dealt with.
