examples.title: Entry points in a college counselling centre
examples.text: One student walks in saying 'I dropped my coaching classes and now my parents are furious' (a failed strategy). Another says 'I just want to feel confident in group discussions' (Stage II, a want). Another says 'Everything is fine, but I feel stuck' (an opportunity). The counsellor begins wherever each student starts.

examples.title: The four questions for a placement worry
examples.text: A final-year student anxious about placements: What's going on? (no internship, weak resume). What does a better future look like? (an offer in a field she likes). How do I get there? (resume clinic, two projects, mock interviews). How do I make it happen? (book the resume clinic this week).

examples.title: Stages of change with phone addiction
examples.text: A student first says 'My screen time is fine' (unawareness), then notices exam scores dropping (initial awareness), admits 'I really need to cut down' (heightened awareness), deletes one app (preliminary action), panics before exams (urgency), and finally sets app limits and a study timetable he actually follows (serious action), with occasional binge nights (lapse).

examples.title: Chaotic action vs orderly inactivity
examples.text: A shy student spends months planning the 'perfect' way to join the college theatre club and never goes. A friend just shows up to an audition, does badly, but learns what to work on. That is Weick's point: acting, even messily, gives you material to learn from.

examples.title: The framework as 'browser'
examples.text: A trainee counsellor reads about mindfulness, CBT thought records and solution-focused 'miracle questions'. Instead of adopting any one wholesale, she asks where each fits (new perspectives? goal setting? action?) and whether it helps her clients' outcomes, keeping only what does.

examples.title: A fad in practice
examples.text: A new 'one-technique-cures-all' workshop goes viral on social media and everyone starts using it. A year later it is forgotten. Egan's advice: note the hot topic, test it, and integrate what is useful into your overall approach.

practice.q: Explain Egan's three-stage problem-management model with its tasks.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Gerard Egan's Skilled Helper approach is a problem-management and opportunity-development framework. Egan argues that every worthwhile helping approach ultimately helps clients answer four questions: What's going on? What does a better future look like? How do I get there? How do I make it all happen? In Figure 8.1 these become three logical stages (the current picture, the preferred picture and the way forward) resting on an action arrow that represents implementation. Each stage has three tasks, framed as questions clients ask themselves.

Stage I: Help clients explore their concerns. The aim is to help clients spell out their concerns as clearly as possible, with neither too much nor too little detail. Task I-A, the story (problem situations), asks: What's going on in my life? What are my main concerns? Task I-B, the real story (new perspectives), asks: As I look more closely, what is really going on, and what new perspectives will help? Task I-C, the right story (key issues), asks: What should I work on? Which issues, if handled well, will make a real difference? Even this exploratory stage should stimulate action towards preferred outcomes.

Stage II: Help clients determine problem-managing outcomes and set goals. Here helpers partner with clients to imagine the future they want. Task II-A, possibilities, asks: What possibilities do I have for a better future, and what do problem-managing outcomes look like? Task II-B, goals/outcomes, asks: What do I really want and need, and what solutions are best for me? Task II-C, commitment, asks: What am I willing to pay for what I want?

Stage III: Help clients draw up plans to accomplish goals. The aim is a realistic plan. Task III-A, possible strategies, asks: What are the possible paths to my goals and what actions will help? Task III-B, best-fit strategies, asks: Which strategy or set of strategies is best for me and fits my resources? Task III-C, plans to accomplish goals, asks: What should my campaign for constructive change look like, and what do I do first, second, third?

Implementation and the action arrow: Clients must turn exploration, goal setting and planning into results and persevere until change happens. All three stages sit on the action arrow, meaning clients should act on their own behalf from the start. Egan stresses that the stages and nine tasks are about planning for change, not change itself; without action they are "blah, blah, blah". Figure 8.3 says action should start immediately, continue throughout and lead to preferred outcomes. Counting the action arrow, there are ten tasks or "moves".

Framework, not rigid model: Egan prefers the word framework because it organises the ingredients of successful therapy, maps the geography of helping, is shared by client and helper, and is systematic but nonlinear, with elastic borders. Drawing on Kay's idea of obliquity, he warns against imposing its linear logic. Clients may enter at any stage, engage with tasks differently and move back and forth as stages intermingle; yet flexibility is not chaos, since the stages act as orientation devices on a shared map. Egan supports the value of an explicit problem-management focus with Lagerveld and colleagues' study, in which work-focused CBT returned workers to their jobs 65 days sooner than standard CBT.

Conclusion: Egan's model gives helper and client a shared map of three stages and nine tasks, built on continuous action. Its strength lies in combining a clear logic with flexibility, so that the client's needs, not the model, guide the helping process.

practice.q: Describe Egan's stages of change and their relevance to client readiness for change.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Egan notes that the problem-management process can be described in terms of the natural stages people pass through when they change, and what they think, feel and do at each. He draws on Yankelovich's seven-step process and on Prochaska and colleagues' five stages (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance), which cover both client-mediated and helper-assisted change. Both are forms of problem management and both show a client's readiness for change. Egan reworks them into thirteen steps.

1. Unawareness: the person is unaware of a problem, vaguely aware, or aware with no intention to act. Sunil tells neighbours complaining about noise that it is their problem. Resistance is the hallmark; there is no readiness.
2. Initial awareness: an issue is noticed but readiness is very low. Clive, with two drink-driving citations, is vaguely aware of legal consequences but does not see himself as a problem drinker.
3. Heightened awareness: the person knows there is a problem and seriously considers change but is ambivalent. William knows he must quit smoking "sooner or later"; change still seems too costly.
4. Preliminary actions: feeble or symbolic attempts, such as William cutting down to eight cigarettes, avoiding temptation and some meagre planning.
5. Urgency: distress grows. Clive, breathalysed after a minor traffic offence, finally sees he is a problem drinker.
6. Search for remedies: strategies are explored and tried, often without weighing costs, for example a couple in a troubled marriage considering complaining, separating, revenge or counselling.
7. Estimation of costs: the costs become clear, and since no option is painless clients often back away.
8. Weighing the costs: because the problem will not go away, retreat is impossible, and choices are compared seriously, often with an inner dialogue between steps 7 and 8.
9. Rational decision: an intellectual decision to pursue a course of action.
10. Rational-emotional decision: the heart joins the head. Decisions driven by conviction and emotion are more likely to lead to action.
11. Serious action: visible, systematic effort to bring dysfunctional behaviour up to an acceptable standard.
12. Maintenance: consolidating gains and avoiding relapse, possibly for life, as when Clive joins Alcoholics Anonymous.
13. Relapse: Egan distinguishes a minor lapse, a relapse and a total collapse. Lapses can teach; a relapse may mean returning to an earlier stage or starting again.

Relevance to helping: Keeping this sequence in mind helps the helper meet clients "where they are" and tailor the problem-management process to their readiness. A client at unawareness needs different help from one weighing costs or one maintaining gains. The stages also explain why clients back away (estimation of costs) and why intellectual agreement alone may not produce action (the need for a rational-emotional decision).

Conclusion: Egan's thirteen steps give a detailed picture of readiness for change, from resistance to maintenance and possible relapse. However, he cautions that this is only a conceptual framework, and becoming preoccupied with any framework is a disservice to clients.

practice.q: Discuss the need for flexibility in using the problem-management process.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Many people reject problem management as "rigid", saying ordinary people do not live that way. Egan insists that the theme of flexibility cannot be overstated. His framework is systematic but nonlinear, with elastic borders, and both rigorous and soft-edged.

Kay's obliquity: Egan draws on economist John Kay's book Obliquity, which argues that problem management, especially changing human behaviour, is best approached indirectly. We rarely know the "moving parts" of important problems; problem management is iterative; people are poor linear thinkers in messy situations; emotions confuse matters; and overly linear processes blind people to facts that contradict their assumptions. Logic should be used with caution and not confused with truth. Egan admits that his I-II-III and A-B-C coding, plus the action arrow, gives ten neat tasks with a linear logic, but says this logic is useful only as far as it serves clients. Helpers should not impose it but learn to use the ten "moves" instinctively and wisely.

1. Clients start and proceed differently: any stage or task can be the entry point. Client A begins with a failed strategy (threatening to quit and being told to leave); Client B with a want (a partner who accepts her), a Stage II entry; Client C with the roots of a problem (childhood abuse), a Stage I entry; Client D with vague dissatisfaction, an opportunity rather than a problem.

2. Clients engage in each stage and task differently: some pour out their story, some leak it in pieces, some tell only flattering parts, and most speak of problems rather than opportunities. So Stage I cannot, and should not, be completed before moving on. Some clients understand problems only by discussing what they want; others must act before they understand. Woody, a college student, went out to "just do it" with dating, failed, and returned with concrete experiences to explore. This illustrates Weick's dictum that chaotic action is sometimes preferable to orderly inactivity.

3. Stages and tasks intermingle: in one session a client may name a problem, set goals and plan strategies, and new concerns may send the process back to exploration. In a few sentences one client mentioned a failed strategy, questioned a goal, hinted at a new problem, raised an issue with the helping relationship, suggested a new approach and recast the problem as an opportunity. The helper must make sense of such entry points and guide the client to whatever stage or task helps.

4. Flexibility is not randomness or chaos: letting clients wander in the name of flexibility leads nowhere. The structure is the foundation for flexibility, the system that keeps helping from being random. Stages and tasks are orientation devices; the framework is a shared map so clients know where they are going.

Conclusion: For Egan, flexibility and structure go together. The framework gives direction, while the helper adapts to the client's entry point, style and movement between stages. As he notes elsewhere, effective models used effectively are liberating rather than controlling.

practice.q: Critically discuss the shadow side of helping models as described by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Egan admits that his framework is rational, linear and systematic, whereas the world is often irrational and chaotic. He argues that rational frameworks help clients bring discipline and order to chaotic lives, especially when culturally flexible, and that helpers should use them unapologetically while letting their humanity permeate them. He then identifies specific shadow-side pitfalls in using any helping model.

1. No model or framework: some helpers "wing it" without a consistent, integrated model, or use problem management without realising it. Trainees who learn many "major brands" but lack their own integrated approach must develop one quickly. Research shows helpers need a method they believe in, are competent in and share with clients.

2. Confusing and needless multiplication of models: there are dozens or hundreds of approaches, all claiming success, with models for almost every disorder, every age group and concepts like mindfulness or strengths. Egan does not dismiss their value but calls for better ways to distil and organise the profession's knowledge.

3. Fads and forgetfulness: a fad is a useful insight marketed alone as the central intervention rather than integrated; it may be a rediscovery. Rachman likens the market for ideas to the share market: it overshoots and crashes. Helpers should integrate useful hot topics, take outrageous claims with a grain of salt and test them. The opposite error, irrational forgetfulness, shelves good ideas, such as the laws of human behaviour (Watson and Tharp) and cognitive dissonance.

4. Failure to share the helping model: some helpers cannot explain the process because they have none; others think it secret, sacred or dangerous, though Duncan and colleagues found no evidence for this. Clients in the driver's seat need to understand the process and make decisions within it.

5. Rigid application of treatment methods: some helpers stop learning and value a model's purity over clients' needs; beginners drag clients linearly through a model. Both are excessive control; effective models used well are liberating.

6. Chaos in defining competence: a 2007 special section proposed "cradle to grave" competence assessment with 15 brutally thorough principles, at times treating helping as an adjunct to medicine. Lichtenberg and colleagues said consensus on competencies is a critical first step. Despite agreement that helping helps and that common factors matter, the profession is still at the starting gate.

7. Failure to grow with the profession: experienced helpers often know little research. Boisvert and Faust found practitioners misjudged research findings and saw much as irrelevant. Cook and colleagues found therapists adopt treatments that fit their existing therapy and are endorsed by respected peers, and keep them if they work and clients like them, suggesting a common-sense scepticism.

8. Ethics of training helpers: Barnett's section addresses the "hot potato" of trainees who lack competence, have behavioural problems or fail ethically. Responsibility gets passed around and some slip through. Better selection is the starting point, despite false positives, false negatives and lawsuits.

Critical evaluation: Egan's list is balanced. He does not reject models but warns against having none, having too many, following them rigidly or keeping them hidden. His remedy is consistent: an integrated, open, shared framework guided by client needs.

Conclusion: The shadow side reminds helpers that models are tools to serve clients. Used flexibly, openly and with ongoing learning, they liberate; used carelessly or rigidly, they harm.

practice.q: Explain integrative eclecticism and how the problem-management framework serves as a 'browser'.
practice.answer:
Introduction: Egan argues that every therapy deals with experiences, cognitions, behaviour and emotions, so all are in a sense cognitive-behavioural-emotive, and problem management is both inherent in every therapy and a valid treatment in itself. Yet no approach will ever be the last word because research keeps challenging or complementing ideas, effective helpers keep seeking better ways to deliver services, and clients expect best practice. This leads to integrative eclecticism: an ongoing search for best practice.

Eclecticism: many experienced helpers borrow methods from other approaches even when loyal to one school; others stitch together their own approach without allegiance to any. This is eclecticism (Corey; Lazarus, Beutler and Norcross; Norcross and Goldfried and others). Milan, Montgomery and Rogers found about 40% of helpers named eclecticism as their primary approach. But effective eclecticism cannot be random borrowing; it needs an integrating framework, and must be systematic.

Pluralism: Cooper and McLeod see their pluralistic approach as a step beyond integrative eclecticism. It rests on the belief that different clients benefit from different things at different times and that therapist and client should work together to identify what the client wants and how to get it. Goals, tasks and methods from many orientations are agreed through dialogue, with the client in the driver's seat. Egan notes that goals, tasks and methods are at the heart of problem management, and that Cooper and McLeod, Duncan and he "sit in the same church, but perhaps in different pews".

The framework as browser: Egan proposes his process as a "browser" for working with ideas from any source:
- Mining: dig out what is useful from any school without accepting everything. The model's philosophy, skills, stages and tasks help identify useful methods.
- Organising: because it is structured by stages and tasks, it can organise mined techniques; for example, techniques from many therapies were organised under identifying blind spots and developing new perspectives.
- Evaluating: because it is pragmatic and outcome-focused, it lets helpers ask how a technique contributes to the bottom line of client outcomes.
- Incorporating: the best ideas are built into the helper's evolving framework, replacing outdated ideas, correcting flawed ones and enhancing viable ones, as each edition of the book has done.
- The client as decision maker: Duncan, Cooper and McLeod and Egan insist clients be involved in all decisions; Egan adds "nudging" and invitations to self-challenge, which he sees as a service rather than "fudging".

Open-systems model: these functions are possible because the framework is an open system, not a closed school. It takes a stand but is open to being corroborated, complemented and challenged by any approach. The needs of clients, not the egos of model builders, stay central.

Conclusion: Integrative eclecticism, for Egan, means systematic, client-focused borrowing held together by the problem-management framework. Used as a browser, the framework lets helpers offer clients best practice whatever its origin.

practice.q: Briefly review the ingredients of successful therapy as summarised by Egan at the start of Part III.
practice.answer:
Egan presents the problem-management approach as the organiser of the ingredients of successful therapy. (1) The client and the context of the client's life are the centrepiece; the client stays in the driver's seat. (2) The person of the therapist matters as a competent consultant and catalyst, but the client, not the therapist, is the main character. (3) The helping relationship is collaborative, not an equal partnership, since the client's problems are the focus; helpers succeed only as far as clients do. (4) The therapeutic dialogue relies on communication skills that are central to the helper's consultant role. (5) Two-way feedback: therapy is client-directed and outcome-informed (Duncan and colleagues), with session-to-session feedback on progress and usefulness. (6) The standard problem-management process is a human universal, used in nearly every therapy and easily understood by clients. (7) The model or method of treatment: problem management is itself an experiential-cognitive-behavioural-emotive method. (8) Decision making is a human universal at the heart of problem management. (9) Beliefs, values, norms, ethics and morality run through all behaviour and add messiness, but are central to therapy.

Egan concludes that the primary integrative process is simply a client successfully managing a problem situation.

practice.q: Explain the significance of the 'action arrow' in Egan's model.
practice.answer:
Implementation asks how clients turn exploration, goal setting and planning into results and keep going until change happens. Egan says helping is about change, and change demands effort.

All three stages sit on the action arrow, showing that clients should act on their own behalf from the very beginning rather than waiting until a plan is complete. The arrow reminds helpers that every stage is about outcomes and their impact on clients' lives, and the bias for action from Chapter 2 should permeate every stage and task.

Egan points out that Stage I deals with issues calling for change, and Stages II and III with planning for change; the three stages and nine tasks are therefore planning, not change itself. Without goal-accomplishing action, talking about problems, goals and strategies is "blah, blah, blah"; change does not emerge magically but through hard work. Still, every stage can promote action, and helpers should build action into planning and planning into action, encouraging "little actions" early.

Figure 8.3 summarises that action should start immediately, continue throughout the process and lead to the client's preferred outcomes. With the action arrow, the framework has ten tasks or "moves".

practice.q: Why does Egan prefer the term 'framework' to 'model'?
practice.answer:
Egan explains his choice in relation to Figure 8.2. First, the framework organises all the ingredients of successful therapy from Chapter 1. Second, it lays out the geography of problem management, helping clients and therapists know where they are in the flow of helping. Third, it is owned by both client and helper, so it promotes dialogue and collaboration. Fourth, although it has an inner logic and is systematic, it is nonlinear, flexible and has elastic borders: clients can move to the stages and tasks they find most useful, and therapists can invite them into helpful areas they overlook. Fifth, it is therefore both rigorous and soft-edged, bending to clients' needs while staying focused on life-enhancing outcomes.

Later Egan adds that the approach is an open-systems model, not a closed school. It takes a stand on how to help, but is open to being corroborated, complemented and challenged by other approaches, which lets it act as a "browser" for mining, organising, evaluating and incorporating techniques. The term framework answers critics who call problem management rigid, and keeps clients' needs, not model builders' egos, at the centre.

practice.q: Write a note on 'How are we doing?': ongoing evaluation of the helping process.
practice.answer:
Given the importance of feedback, Egan asks how helpers can evaluate what is happening with each client. His answer is to treat each case as a "mini-experiment". Psychology has a long history of N = 1, or single-case, designs used both to evaluate practice and for research. It is not enough to know that helping works in general; helpers need to know how well it works in each case.

Lebow describes the single-case design as a more formal, systematic way of documenting what clinicians do anyway, and, like Duncan, recommends questionnaires to record changes in therapy and in daily life. Bangert and Baumberger note that N = 1 is the most relevant design for practising counsellors, yet few are skilled in it.

Many models place evaluation as the last step, but Egan says evaluation only at the end is too late. Mash and Hunsley argued that early detection of what is going wrong prevents failure, and that an early-detection framework should be theory-based, ongoing, practical and sensitive to new perspectives. Egan claims his framework meets these criteria. It is a tool for checking progress throughout helping and provides criteria for helper effectiveness, client participation and outcomes.

practice.q: Explain fads and irrational forgetfulness in the helping professions.
practice.answer:
Egan lists fads and forgetfulness as a shadow-side pitfall of helping models. A fad is an insight or technique that would have merit if integrated into an overall framework, but is instead marketed on its own as the central, or only, meaningful intervention. A fad need not be new; it may be the rediscovery of an old truth or technique that never found its proper place in the tool kit. Rachman compares the market for ideas to the share market: it always overshoots, ideas are pushed beyond their logical conclusions through "irrational exuberance", and then they crash. Helpers become enamoured of such ideas and later abandon them.

Egan's advice is to note hot topics and integrate whatever is useful into a comprehensive approach, and to take the outrageous claims of new approaches with a grain of salt and test them rather than ignore them.

The opposite problem is irrational forgetfulness: good ideas are highlighted for a while and then shelved rather than developed. Examples are the laws of human behaviour based on incentives, rewards and punishment (Watson and Tharp), and cognitive dissonance, rarely discussed now though revived by a popular book (Tarves and Aronson).

practice.q: Explain John Kay's concept of obliquity and its implications for Egan's model.
practice.answer:
John Kay, a British economist, wrote Obliquity, a book broadly about problem management and opportunity development. His thesis is that problem management, especially changing human behaviour, is best pursued indirectly rather than linearly. We rarely know enough about the "moving parts" of important problems to tackle them head-on; problem management evolves and is iterative; people are poor linear thinkers in messy situations, and emotions add confusion. An overly direct process blinds people to facts that contradict their assumptions, so logic and linearity can obstruct common sense and good intuition, and can lock people into preferred rather than effective solutions. Kay advises using logic with caution and not confusing logic with truth.

Egan applies this to his own framework. The stages and tasks are coded I, II, III and A, B, C and, with the action arrow, form ten neatly packaged tasks that suggest linear logic. Egan says this logic must never be overstated; it is useful only to the extent it serves clients. Helpers should not be fooled by it or impose it on clients but let clients' needs guide them, using the ten "moves" instinctively and wisely. This leads to his four points on flexibility.

Obliquity is the title and thesis of a book by British economist John Kay: problem management, especially changing human behaviour, is best pursued indirectly rather than in a straight line, because we rarely understand all the moving parts. Egan uses it to warn against imposing his model's linear logic on clients.

The pluralistic perspective of Cooper and McLeod is the belief that different clients benefit from different things at different times, and that therapists should work closely with clients to identify what they want from therapy and how to get it. Goals, tasks and methods are agreed through dialogue.

An N = 1 or single-case design treats each client's case as a mini-experiment to evaluate how well helping is working for that individual. Lebow calls it a systematic way of documenting what clinicians already do; Bangert and Baumberger say few counsellors are adept at it.

Weick's dictum is that chaotic action is sometimes preferable to orderly inactivity. Egan illustrates it with Woody, whose failed dating attempts taught him about himself and gave concrete material for exploring his interpersonal style.

practice.q: Name Prochaska's five stages of change.
practice.answer: Prochaska and colleagues describe five stages of client-mediated and helper-assisted change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. Egan combines this with Yankelovich's seven steps into his own thirteen-step sequence.

practice.q: What did Lagerveld et al. (2012) find?
practice.answer: Among about 170 workers off work with common mental health problems, those given work-focused CBT with a problem-management, return-to-work emphasis went back to work about 65 days sooner than those given standard CBT.

practice.q: What is a fad in helping?
practice.answer: A fad is an insight or technique that would have merit if integrated into a wider framework but is marketed alone as the central or only intervention. It can even be the rediscovery of an old idea. Egan advises testing such claims and integrating what is useful.
